analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal workplace safety inspections, citations, and penalties under OSHA.
analysis.headline: A bill that would have repealed OSHA's inspection and penalty powers, backed by 14 House Republicans, died in a House subcommittee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have deleted the sections of the Occupational Safety and Health Act that let federal inspectors examine workplaces, issue citations, enforce safety rules in court, and fine or prosecute employers who break safety laws. It would have kept OSHA's power to write safety standards but made following them essentially voluntary. In exchange, it offered small businesses a government-funded consulting and training program, legalized employer-run safety committees, and created awards for companies with good safety records.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially in hazardous industries like construction and manufacturing, would no longer face federal safety inspections, citations, court enforcement, or civil and criminal penalties for violating workplace safety rules. Small employers would gain a new federally funded assistance and training program, guaranteed at least one-quarter of OSHA's annual budget. Companies with strong safety records could win a federal award they could use in advertising.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the OSHA provisions for inspections, investigations, recordkeeping, citations, enforcement procedures, judicial review, and civil and criminal penalties, leaving no federal mechanism to find or punish workplace safety violations.

It establishes a small business assistance and training program with technical and consultative services targeted at small employers and the most hazardous industries, funded by at least one-fourth of OSHA's annual appropriation.

It declares that employer-employee safety committees are not 'labor organizations' under the National Labor Relations Act, allowing companies to set up workplace safety committees without union involvement.
It adds cost-benefit and feasibility requirements that every new OSHA standard must satisfy, and creates an award program that winning companies may publicize in advertising.

analysis.who_pays: Workers in dangerous jobs would bear the cost: no federal inspector could enter their workplace, no citation could be issued for a violation, and no fine or criminal penalty could be brought against an employer who ignored safety standards. Safety rules would still exist on paper, but compliance would depend entirely on employers' voluntary cooperation.

drawbacks.text: Repealing every inspection, citation, and penalty provision would leave OSHA standards with no enforcement mechanism, meaning a rule is only as strong as an employer's willingness to follow it voluntarily.

The small business assistance program, while real, is funded from OSHA's existing budget — one-fourth of the same appropriation that would no longer support inspections — so safety help would come at the expense of safety enforcement.

Supporters' good-faith argument was that OSHA inspections and penalties impose real costs, particularly on small businesses, and that consultation, training, and recognition of good performers could improve safety without adversarial enforcement; the bill also imposed stricter cost-benefit tests on new standards to filter out rules whose costs outweigh their benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine benefits — free safety consulting for small businesses, employer-employee safety committees, and awards for good performers — are modest next to the core change: stripping the government of every tool to detect and punish workplace safety violations. The bill keeps OSHA's standard-setting power but makes compliance voluntary, which historically leaves the worst actors unchecked while good employers gain nothing they didn't already have.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to its Workforce Protections subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Joel Hefley of Colorado introduced the OSHA Reform Act of 1999 on March 18, 1999, with 12 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
On April 9, 1999, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, which was the last action ever taken on it.
The bill received no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate action before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, which favored working people here: federal workplace inspections, citations, and penalties remained in force because the bill never advanced. The employers who would have been freed from safety enforcement gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept federal safety enforcement

for.name: Rep. Joel Hefley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal OSHA's inspection, citation, enforcement, and penalty provisions.

for.name: 13 of 222 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 14 sponsors were Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Workforce Protections subcommittee on April 9, 1999, and never acted on it further.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill never advanced far enough for Democrats or any other members to take a recorded position on it.

industries.industry: Employers in hazardous industries (construction, manufacturing, meatpacking)
industries.note: The bill would have eliminated federal inspections, citations, and civil and criminal penalties, so safety violations would carry no federal consequence. The gain comes directly out of workers' protection on the job.

Small employers would get a federally funded consulting and training program guaranteed at least one-fourth of OSHA's budget, and they would be exempt from penalties. The assistance is a real benefit, but it is paid for by diverting the agency's resources away from enforcement.

The bill declares employer-run safety committees are not 'labor organizations' under the National Labor Relations Act, letting companies address safety through management-led committees rather than union representation. Workers' independent voice on safety would be weakened alongside the unions'.
